items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sustainability"?
options: Having reliable, affordable access to enough energy
Electricity generated from the heat released by splitting uranium atoms
The using up of a resource faster than it is replaced
Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
items.answer: Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
items.markingKey: D. "sustainability" is meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "audience"?
options: A note-taking method that divides the page into a notes column, a cue column of key questions and a summary
The people for whom a piece of work is intended, which affects style and vocabulary
A testable statement that predicts the answer to a research question
The limits of an investigation, such as the place, time period and group studied
items.answer: The people for whom a piece of work is intended, which affects style and vocabulary
items.markingKey: B. "audience" is the people for whom a piece of work is intended, which affects style and vocabulary.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A US satellite navigation system in which receivers calculate their position from the signals of at least four satellites"?
options: data layer
Global Positioning System (GPS)
remote sensing
contour line
items.answer: Global Positioning System (GPS)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Global Positioning System (GPS).

items.stem: Distinguish between a primary source and a secondary source.
items.answer: A primary source comes from the time or from a witness (e.g. a diary, a law code); a secondary source is a later interpretation by someone who was not there (e.g. a textbook).
items.markingKey: A primary source comes from the time or from a witness (e.g. a diary, a law code); a secondary source is a later interpretation by someone who was not there (e.g. a textbook). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a ryot under the ryotwari system and a zamindar under the Permanent Settlement.
items.answer: Under the Permanent Settlement, zamindars were made landowners responsible for paying a fixed revenue; under the ryotwari system (Madras, Bombay) peasants (ryots) paid revenue directly to the state.
items.markingKey: Under the Permanent Settlement, zamindars were made landowners responsible for paying a fixed revenue; under the ryotwari system (Madras, Bombay) peasants (ryots) paid revenue directly to the state. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between active resistance and passive resistance.
items.answer: Active resistance includes revolts and escape (e.g. the Haitian Revolution, maroon communities); passive resistance includes working slowly, damaging tools and keeping culture, language and religion alive.
items.markingKey: Active resistance includes revolts and escape (e.g. the Haitian Revolution, maroon communities); passive resistance includes working slowly, damaging tools and keeping culture, language and religion alive. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – Book extract (paraphrased): Paraphrase of arguments made by Arno Peters, a German historian, in "The New Cartography" (1983)

The familiar world map greatly overstates the size of the countries of the North, which were mainly colonial powers, and understates the size of the countries of Africa, Asia and Latin America. A map that shows every country in its true proportion of area is needed for a fairer picture of the world.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about map types and map projections. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of arguments made by Arno Peters, a German historian, in "The New Cartography" (1983). Purpose: to persuade readers that the Mercator projection is biased and that his own equal-area projection should replace it. Value: It clearly shows the perspective of the main promoter of the Gall–Peters projection and the political argument behind it. Limitation: Peters was promoting his own map, so he does not mention that equal-area maps also distort shape or that earlier cartographers had designed similar projections.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of arguments made by Arno Peters, a German historian, in "The New Cartography" (1983). Purpose: to persuade readers that the Mercator projection is biased and that his own equal-area projection should replace it. Value: It clearly shows the perspective of the main promoter of the Gall–Peters projection and the political argument behind it. Limitation: Peters was promoting his own map, so he does not mention that equal-area maps also distort shape or that earlier cartographers had designed similar projections. items.stem:
Source A – Business report (paraphrased): Summary of news reports on mechanisation of tea picking in Kericho, Kenya, 2010s–2020s

A survey of tea estates found that hand-picking remains common because skilled pickers select only the top leaves, giving higher-quality tea. Some estates have introduced picking machines, which cut costs but have led to protests by workers worried about losing their jobs.

According to Source A, what can we learn about the factors of production and the three economic questions? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: Kenyan tea estates face a choice between skilled hand-picking and cheaper machines that threaten jobs.
items.markingKey: Kenyan tea estates face a choice between skilled hand-picking and cheaper machines that threaten jobs. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [5]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem:
Source A – Student reflection (paraphrased): Reflection written by a Grade 8 student in an MYP I&S process journal, 2024

My first question was "What is climate change?" My teacher said it was too broad. I changed it to "How has the length of the dry season changed in Chennai since 1990?" Now I could find rainfall data from the Indian Meteorological Department and compare it with news reports.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on scarcity, needs and wants and opportunity cost produced the question "Is money important?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed, vague value question Improved: "How do students at our school decide how to spend their weekly pocket money, and what do they give up?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed, vague value question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How do students at our school decide how to spend their weekly pocket money, and what do they give up?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Maya is investigating the motives and voyages of European exploration and proposes the research question: "Who was the best explorer?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is an opinion question without criteria and ignores causes Improved: "Why did Portugal, rather than Spain, reach India by sea first, between 1415 and 1498?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is an opinion question without criteria and ignores causes); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "Why did Portugal, rather than Spain, reach India by sea first, between 1415 and 1498?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Mateo argues that "Physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining population distribution." Hana disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive.
items.markingKey: Mateo: climate, water and relief set limits – deserts, ice caps and mountains are sparsely populated. Hana: jobs and services in cities draw people regardless of physical conditions, e.g. Dubai. Judgement (1-2 marks): At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why societies need rules and laws.
items.answer: Laws keep order and protect people's safety, rights and property, settle disputes peacefully, and make expectations clear so people can cooperate.
items.markingKey: Content: Laws keep order and protect people's safety, rights and property, settle disputes peacefully, and make expectations clear so people can cooperate. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: "Earthquakes are more dangerous than volcanoes." Discuss.
items.answer: Generally true for loss of life because earthquakes cannot be predicted, but the danger of either depends on the size of the event and the vulnerability of the people affected.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: earthquakes strike with almost no warning; they have caused most of the deadliest disasters, e.g. Haiti 2010 and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Arguments against: volcanoes can be deadly and affect the whole world, such as Tambora in 1815; ash clouds, lahars and gases have long-lasting impacts. Supported judgement: Generally true for loss of life because earthquakes cannot be predicted, but the danger of either depends on the size of the event and the vulnerability of the people affected. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: "Hydraulic action is the most important process of river erosion." Discuss.
items.answer: Not always: the most important process depends on rock type, load and discharge; abrasion is often dominant in high-energy rivers carrying sediment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is powerful in floods and where water is forced into cracks; it widens joints and plucks rock from banks. Arguments against: abrasion often removes more material, especially in rivers with a lot of load; solution is dominant on limestone. Supported judgement: Not always: the most important process depends on rock type, load and discharge; abrasion is often dominant in high-energy rivers carrying sediment. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hard engineering"?
options: Erosion in which rocks carried by the river knock into each other and become smaller and rounder
A bend in a river, with fast flow and erosion on the outside and slow flow and deposition on the inside
Building structures such as dams, levees and flood walls to control rivers
A landform of deposited sediment at a river mouth, where the river splits into smaller channels (distributaries)
items.answer: Building structures such as dams, levees and flood walls to control rivers
items.markingKey: C. "hard engineering" is building structures such as dams, levees and flood walls to control rivers.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "theocracy"?
options: A state governed by religious leaders or according to religious law
A system in which a hereditary monarch is head of state but power is limited by a constitution and an elected parliament
The principle that everyone, including leaders, is subject to the same laws, applied fairly by independent courts
A duty that a person is expected to carry out, such as obeying the law or respecting others' rights
items.answer: A state governed by religious leaders or according to religious law
items.markingKey: A. "theocracy" is a state governed by religious leaders or according to religious law.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "caravanserai"?
options: The writing system of ancient Egypt that used pictures and symbols
The movement of tools, techniques and knowledge from one society to another
A roadside inn with a courtyard where merchants and their animals rested on Silk Road routes
A number system in which the value of a digit depends on its position, such as tens and hundreds
items.answer: A roadside inn with a courtyard where merchants and their animals rested on Silk Road routes
items.markingKey: C. "caravanserai" is a roadside inn with a courtyard where merchants and their animals rested on Silk Road routes.

items.stem: "Indigenous Americans died mainly in battles with Europeans." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Disease killed far more than warfare, although violence, forced labour and displacement also caused many deaths.
items.markingKey: Disease killed far more than warfare, although violence, forced labour and displacement also caused many deaths. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why tectonic plates move.
items.answer: Heat from the Earth's core drives convection in the mantle; ridge push at spreading ridges and slab pull at subduction zones move the plates a few centimetres a year. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Heat from the Earth's core drives convection in the mantle; ridge push at spreading ridges and slab pull at subduction zones move the plates a few centimetres a year. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a hypothesis and a research question.
items.answer: A research question asks what you want to find out; a hypothesis is a prediction of the answer that the investigation will test.
items.markingKey: A research question asks what you want to find out; a hypothesis is a prediction of the answer that the investigation will test. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – Ancient history (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Herodotus, "The Histories", Book II, written c. 430 BCE

The Greek writer described Egypt as a land made by the river: each year the Nile flooded the fields, and when the waters went down the Egyptians sowed their crops in the rich mud it left behind.

According to Source A, what can we learn about chronology, BCE/CE dating and timelines? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: Egyptian farming and civilisation depended on the annual Nile flood.
items.markingKey: Egyptian farming and civilisation depended on the annual Nile flood. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [5]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem:
Source A – UN convention (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Article 28 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, 1989

States shall make primary education compulsory and available free to all; encourage different forms of secondary education and make them available to every child; and take measures to encourage regular attendance at school and reduce drop-out rates.

What is the message of Source A about citizens' rights and responsibilities, including children's rights under the UNCRC? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: States must provide free primary education and encourage all children to attend school.
items.markingKey: States must provide free primary education and encourage all children to attend school. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [5]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem:
Source A – Government report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the announcement by the Canadian Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, 2 July 1992

The minister announced a moratorium on the northern cod fishery. Scientists had found that the spawning stock had fallen to the lowest level ever measured. The closure would affect thousands of fishers and plant workers, and the government would provide income support.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on map skills such as grid references, scale and direction produced the question "What are maps?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed, very broad definition question with no place, group or measurable focus Improved: "How accurately do students at our school estimate walking distances compared with measurements from a 1:25 000 map?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed, very broad definition question with no place, group or measurable focus); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How accurately do students at our school estimate walking distances compared with measurements from a 1:25 000 map?" items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What are factors of production?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into the factors of production and the three economic questions. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it only asks for a definition Improved: "Why do some coffee farms in Colombia use labour-intensive methods while large farms in Brazil use machines?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it only asks for a definition); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "Why do some coffee farms in Colombia use labour-intensive methods while large farms in Brazil use machines?" items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why the doctrine of lapse created resentment among Indian rulers.
items.answer: It let the Company annex states such as Jhansi and Satara when a ruler had no natural son, ignoring the Indian custom of adoption, so rulers feared losing their lands.
items.markingKey: Content: It let the Company annex states such as Jhansi and Satara when a ruler had no natural son, ignoring the Indian custom of adoption, so rulers feared losing their lands. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. items.stem: Nia argues that ""Gold" was the most important motive for European exploration." Amara disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Economic gain was the strongest motive overall, but it was intertwined with religious and political aims that rulers used to justify expeditions.
items.markingKey: Nia: the spice trade and gold promised huge profits. Amara: spreading Christianity was a sincere motive for rulers like Isabella. Judgement (1-2 marks): Economic gain was the strongest motive overall, but it was intertwined with religious and political aims that rulers used to justify expeditions.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Rivers were the single most important reason why the first civilisations developed."
items.answer: Rivers were a necessary condition, but not sufficient: civilisation also needed social organisation, technology and trade.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: all four early civilisations grew in river valleys; rivers gave water, silt and transport needed for a food surplus. Arguments against: organisation, leadership and religion turned farming villages into cities; trade and technology such as writing and bronze were also essential. Supported judgement: Rivers were a necessary condition, but not sufficient: civilisation also needed social organisation, technology and trade. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem:
Source A – Mathematical text (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the opening of Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci), "Liber Abaci", 1202

The author explained that with the nine Indian figures and the sign 0, which the Arabs call zephirum, any number at all can be written. He set out how merchants could use the method for calculating prices, weights and exchanges of money.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Paper was the most important technology to travel along the Silk Road."
items.answer: A strong case, because paper underpinned learning, government and printing, but gunpowder and numerals had equally deep effects in other areas.
items.markingKey: From the source: Indian numerals with zero can write any number and are useful for trade. Own knowledge for: it made books and records cheaper and spread learning and bureaucracy; it later enabled the printing revolution. Own knowledge against: gunpowder transformed warfare and the power of states; numerals changed trade, science and mathematics. Judgement: A strong case, because paper underpinned learning, government and printing, but gunpowder and numerals had equally deep effects in other areas. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "When a river overflows its banks and covers land that is normally dry"?
options: levee
flood
gorge
saltation
items.answer: flood
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of flood.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "energy mix"?
options: Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
The combination of energy sources a country uses
Energy from sources that are naturally replenished, such as solar, wind, hydro, geothermal and tidal
Having reliable, affordable access to enough energy
items.answer: The combination of energy sources a country uses
items.markingKey: B. "energy mix" is the combination of energy sources a country uses.

items.stem: On a Mercator map, Greenland looks about the same size as Africa. In reality Africa is about how many times larger?
options: About the same size
About 14 times
About 100 times
About 2 times
items.answer: About 14 times
items.markingKey: B. Africa covers about 30.4 million km²; Greenland about 2.2 million km².

items.stem: A student claims: "The Mughal Empire was poor compared with Europe." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Around 1700 Mughal India was one of the world's largest economies, famed for textiles, and its revenues dwarfed those of most European states.
items.markingKey: Around 1700 Mughal India was one of the world's largest economies, famed for textiles, and its revenues dwarfed those of most European states. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Child labour started with the Industrial Revolution." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Children had always worked on farms and in domestic industry; factories made their work more visible and regimented.
items.markingKey: Children had always worked on farms and in domestic industry; factories made their work more visible and regimented. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "The East India Company was run by the British government from the start." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It was a private joint-stock company; Parliament gradually regulated it (e.g. Regulating Act 1773) but only took over in 1858.
items.markingKey: It was a private joint-stock company; Parliament gradually regulated it (e.g. Regulating Act 1773) but only took over in 1858. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Development must meet present needs, especially of the poor, without harming future generations.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "Why did Manchester grow so quickly between 1770 and 1850?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Collect census data (1801–1851); research the Bridgewater Canal, cotton mills and the Liverpool–Manchester Railway; read contemporary descriptions; organise causes in a diagram; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect census data (1801–1851); research the Bridgewater Canal, cotton mills and the Liverpool–Manchester Railway; read contemporary descriptions; organise causes in a diagram; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How accurately do students at our school estimate walking distances compared with measurements from a 1:25 000 map?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Choose a route; measure it on a 1:25 000 map using string and the scale bar; survey 20 students for estimates; walk the route with a GPS app; compare results in a table and graph; evaluate measurement errors.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Choose a route; measure it on a 1:25 000 map using string and the scale bar; survey 20 students for estimates; walk the route with a GPS app; compare results in a table and graph; evaluate measurement errors. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Nia argues that "The steam engine was the most important invention of the Industrial Revolution." Diego disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: It was the most transformative single invention, but it depended on earlier inventions and resources, and spread only gradually.
items.markingKey: Nia: it powered factories, mines, trains and ships. Diego: textile machines such as the water frame started the factory system. Judgement (1-2 marks): It was the most transformative single invention, but it depended on earlier inventions and resources, and spread only gradually.

items.stem: Felix argues that "Democracy is always the best form of government." Mohammed disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Democracy is the system most likely to protect rights and accountability, but it works well only with the rule of law, protected minorities and informed citizens.
items.markingKey: Felix: it protects rights and lets citizens remove leaders peacefully. Mohammed: decisions can be slow and short-term. Judgement (1-2 marks): Democracy is the system most likely to protect rights and accountability, but it works well only with the rule of law, protected minorities and informed citizens.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The benefits of industrialisation were shared fairly around the world."
items.answer: Disagree: industrialisation brought wealth mainly to industrialised nations and their elites, while many colonies bore costs, creating a gap that still shapes development.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it eventually raised incomes and produced cheaper goods worldwide; railways and technology spread to many countries. Arguments against: colonies supplied raw materials and lost industries such as Indian textiles; industrial countries grew far richer, widening global inequality. Supported judgement: Disagree: industrialisation brought wealth mainly to industrialised nations and their elites, while many colonies bore costs, creating a gap that still shapes development. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Rapid population growth is the main cause of poverty in low-income countries."
items.answer: Thesis: Disagree: rapid growth can make development harder, but poverty has many causes and often drives high fertility itself.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fast growth puts pressure on schools, health care, jobs and land; young dependants reduce savings per person. Counter-arguments: poverty often causes high birth rates rather than the reverse; governance, conflict, trade and history are major causes of poverty. Thesis/conclusion: Disagree: rapid growth can make development harder, but poverty has many causes and often drives high fertility itself. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).
